Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
The patient is a 57-year-old male with a history of extensive tobacco use, nonischemic cardiomyopathy, and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS) of 3.

Hospital Course:
The patient received mechanical cardiac support with an LVAD due to severe heart failure after successfully completing initial evaluation. Three months after the surgery, mediastinal widening was noted on a chest X-ray performed for dyspnea and cough. CT scans revealed mediastinal lymphadenopathy without evidence of disease outside the chest. Mediastinoscopy was performed and pathologic examination showed consistent SCLC. 

Treatment Strategy:
The patient was removed from active consideration for cardiac transplantation. Chemotherapy was administered while hospitalized for close monitoring. Carboplatin and IV etoposide were given. After his first cycle of chemotherapy, the patient elected not to receive further chemotherapy and workup.

Complications:
The treatment course was complicated by cellulitis, neutropenic fevers with pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, and protracted nausea and vomiting. The patient was treated with a prolonged IV antibiotic course. Although the renal function remained within normal limits, the patient developed signs of worsening overload with left-sided pleural effusion and peripheral edema. 

Outcome: 
The patient elected for hospice care and was discharged home. The patient passed away about 6 months after the administration of chemotherapy.

The patient presented with complaints of burning, itching, pain, stinging, lacrimation, and decreased vision in her left eye. She reported sand splash to her eyes at the seaside three months prior and had discontinued contact lens wear ten days before admission to the clinic. Biomicroscopic examination of the left eye revealed central keratitis and corneal scraping sample was taken and inoculated for testing. Acanthamoeba sp. cysts were identified in the direct Giemsa stained specimen of corneal scraping. 

Treatment: 
The patient was treated with alternating topical fortified vancomycin, ceftazidime, propamidine isothionate 0.1% and chlorhexidine at ophthalmology clinic. Contact lenses and contact lens solution could not be cultured since they had been disposed of by the patient.

Follow-up: 
At the 2nd month visit, no growth was identified after inoculation of corneal scraping specimen onto E. coli plated NNA agar. The corneal scraping specimen was defined as "T2" genotype "A. castellani" according to PCR and sequence analysis that targeted 18S rDNA region performed.

The patient was a 39-year-old male who presented with low back pain without any identified cause, as well as chest pain, right hip pain, and bilateral foot pain. One year later, he developed enlarging soft masses in the plantar side of his right hallux. The patient had no family history of metabolic bone diseases. Upon initial lab testing, the patient had normal calcium levels, but low phosphorus levels and elevated alkaline phosphatase levels. Further testing revealed a significantly elevated level of FGF23, indicating the possibility of TIO.

A systemic venous sampling was conducted to measure the FGF23 in the patient's right common iliac vein and right external iliac vein, which confirmed the diagnosis. The tumors of the flexor tendon were resected, along with a tumor found in the first distal phalanx. Histological examination of the tumors showed oval-shaped mesenchymal cells densely packed in a fibrous background. Mitotic activity and necrosis were absent.

Post-surgery, the patient's serum FGF23 levels dramatically decreased from 215 pg/mL to 47 pg/mL, with phosphorus levels returning to normal. The patient's pain gradually improved over the course of two months and had fully resolved upon discharge.

Clinical Presentation: The patient presented with persistent numbness and burning sensation over the right anterolateral thigh for 2 months.

Medical History: The patient had a history of minor back trauma over 30 years ago, and had well-controlled asthma on regular Seretide inhalers. She was a non-smoker and a teetotaller.

Diagnosis: Meralgia paresthetica.

Treatment: The patient was prescribed pregabalin 75-mg nocte and naproxen 275-mg twice daily to control the paraesthesia, but this offered her no relief. The patient reported the paraesthesia had resolved completely and spontaneously without further treatment.

Nerve Conduction Study: A nerve conduction study of both the right and left LFCNs showed similar results in the latency, amplitude and conduction velocity.

Imaging: A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbosacral plexus using the routine lumbar plexus protocol revealed mild focal swelling in the right LFCN proximal to the foramen beneath the inguinal ligament adjacent to the anterior superior iliac spine, compatible with underlying meralgia paresthetica.
